The ICE name verify_ctor_sanity strongly suggests C++ constructor/object-model validation rather than a target backend problem, and gcc/cp owns constexpr evaluation, class/object semantics, ctor/dtor handling, and lowering of accepted C++ constructs.

The reproducer centers on prvalue/constructor/destructor behavior under optimization, and tree-core owns shared tree-based lowering and canonical transformations including object/lifetime-sensitive middle-end machinery such as inlining/body copying and tree-level transformations. If the front end produces malformed tree representation for ctor/dtor or prvalue materialization, or if shared tree transformations later violate ctor invariants, this module is a plausible intermediate mechanism.

The bug triggers only with optimization enabled (-O/-O1), and pass tracing shows the compilation proceeds through a substantial tree pipeline. gcc/root/gimple owns GIMPLE lowering, builders, validation, and SSA-oriented middle-end machinery used after C++ frontend lowering. If verify_ctor_sanity is checking correctness after gimplification or early tree/GIMPLE transformations, this module is a strong optimization-stage candidate.

Because the ICE is optimization-sensitive and the pass trace shows many tree passes reached, tree-ssa is a plausible intermediate compiler mechanism where optimized SSA-form transformations expose or corrupt ctor-related invariants originating from C++ constexpr/prvalue lowering. [gcc/tree-ssa-dom.cc] Constant/copy propagation into statements is directly tied to optimization-only miscompilations or ICEs caused by replacing operands in forms that are not semantically safe for non-trivial C++ objects. Even without bodies, this function is a high-value suspicious intermediate mechanism because propagating values into ctor/dtor-sensitive statements could trigger malformed IR later checked by verify_ctor_sanity.

ranked_methods.signature: static void verify_ctor_sanity (const constexpr_ctx *ctx, tree type)
ranked_methods.reason: Direct surface-trigger match: the issue summary explicitly names an ICE in verify_ctor_sanity. The body is a tight cluster of gcc_assert checks over constexpr constructor state: ctx->ctor must exist, its type must match the object/type under construction, and ctx->global->get_value (ctx->object) must equal ctx->ctor. For a constexpr C++20 prvalue/non-trivial object regression, this is the most immediate failure site and the best localization target.

ranked_methods.signature: static tree cxx_eval_bare_aggregate (const constexpr_ctx *ctx, tree t, value_cat lval, bool *non_constant_p, bool *overflow_p)
ranked_methods.reason: Strongest immediate upstream source to rank above general dispatchers. This function calls verify_ctor_sanity directly near entry, then constructs and mutates CONSTRUCTOR state for aggregate/union/vector constexpr evaluation, creates sub-constructors, manages active union members, handles empty subobjects, and updates TREE_CONSTANT/TREE_SIDE_EFFECTS flags. A malformed ctor/object mapping here would naturally trip verify_ctor_sanity, making it the closest producer of the bad state.

ranked_methods.signature: static void init_subob_ctx (const constexpr_ctx *ctx, constexpr_ctx &new_ctx, tree index, tree &value)
ranked_methods.reason: Very strong local upstream helper for the failing sanity check. It prepares subobject constexpr context by deriving new_ctx.object with build_ctor_subob_ref, deciding when subobjects get their own CONSTRUCTOR, suppressing empty-subobject slots, and stripping TARGET_EXPR initialization layers. Since verify_ctor_sanity checks object/ctor/type coherence, bugs in subobject context setup are highly plausible for no_unique_address/empty-subobject/prvalue regressions.

ranked_methods.signature: static tree cxx_eval_call_expression (const constexpr_ctx *ctx, tree t, value_cat lval, bool *non_constant_p, bool *overflow_p)
ranked_methods.reason: Major upstream constructor/lifetime engine in constexpr evaluation. The body explicitly creates ctor/object state for constructor AGGR_INIT_EXPR calls, binds constructor/destructor objects, handles TARGET_EXPR-like object materialization, toggles object constness around constructors/destructors, and in C++20 intentionally preserves CONSTRUCTOR_NO_CLEARING for constexpr constructors. That last comment is especially relevant to a C++20 regression involving partially initialized objects and later ctor sanity assertions.

ranked_methods.signature: static tree cxx_eval_constant_expression (const constexpr_ctx *ctx, tree t, value_cat lval, bool *non_constant_p, bool *overflow_p, tree *jump_target )
ranked_methods.reason: Central dispatcher for all constexpr evaluation and the caller path that reaches the failing region. It creates new ctor/object contexts for DECL_EXPR and TARGET_EXPR of aggregate/vector types, routes CONSTRUCTOR nodes into cxx_eval_bare_aggregate, and invokes verify_constructor_flags on reduced constant constructors before re-evaluating them. Although broader and less localized than the top four, its body clearly orchestrates the problematic ctor/object state model.

Important adjacent surface/intermediate checker for constructor consistency. While the reported ICE names verify_ctor_sanity rather than this routine, cxx_eval_constant_expression explicitly calls verify_constructor_flags on constant CONSTRUCTOR nodes. Its body validates TREE_CONSTANT and TREE_SIDE_EFFECTS against constructor elements, so inconsistent constructor metadata from constexpr building could also surface here or nearby. Less likely than the cp/constexpr-specific sanity path, but highly relevant.

Relevant shared constructor-state maintenance routine. Multiple hot candidates, especially cxx_eval_bare_aggregate and gimplify/vector code, manually manipulate or depend on constructor flags; this helper recomputes those flags from elements. If a regression changed how partially initialized constexpr constructors are assembled, stale or mismatched flags here could contribute to later sanity failures. More generic than the cp/constexpr methods, so ranked lower.

ranked_methods.signature: static enum gimplify_status gimplify_init_constructor (tree *expr_p, gimple_seq *pre_p, gimple_seq *post_p, bool want_value, bool notify_temp_creation)
ranked_methods.reason: Best middle-end candidate, but weaker than the constexpr front-end cluster because the named failure is in cp/constexpr and the issue domain is constexpr. Still, the body is highly relevant: it lowers CONSTRUCTOR assignments, reasons about CONSTRUCTOR_NO_CLEARING, complete vs incomplete constructors, zero-clearing, padding, and scalarization/block-copy decisions. If front-end-produced constructors are malformed, this function is a plausible place where optimization-only behavior exposes them.

Narrow but relevant C++ lowering hook. It strips/elides TARGET_EXPR initialization, rewrites AGGR_INIT_EXPR/VEC_INIT_EXPR slots to the destination object, and replaces placeholders for aggregate NSDMI. Because the reproducer is about constexpr prvalues and object materialization, this is a plausible optimization-sensitive lowering point, though still downstream of the stronger constexpr evaluator methods where the named ICE occurs.

Best optimization-pass candidate from the tree-SSA side because it explicitly rewrites constructor assignments. The body handles clobbers, zero-initialization of scalarized subtrees, and removal/modification of aggregate constructor assignments. This is less compelling than the cp/constexpr path because the failure is explicitly in verify_ctor_sanity and pass_trace gives no failing pass, but if optimization is required to expose the bug, constructor-assignment rewriting is one of the most semantically aligned middle-end candidates.
